newsitem.title: PERU: Fujimori to discuss hostage crisis in Bolivia.
newsitem.headline: Fujimori to discuss hostage crisis in Bolivia.

text.p: President Alberto Fujimori, his efforts to end Peru's 108-day hostage crisis at an impasse, was to go to neighbouring Bolivia on Friday for talks on the standoff with Bollivian President Gonzalo Sanchez de Lozada.
Fujimori will arrive in Santa Cruz on Friday night and brief Sanchez de Lozada on the progress -- or lack of progress -- in talks to free the 72 hostages held by leftist guerrillas, officials said.
Bolivia's Ambassador to Peru, Jorge Gumucio, is one of the men held since Dec. 17, 1996, by Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels at the Japanese ambassador's house.

Bolivia has four MRTA militants in its jails, and MRTA is demanding their freedom in exchange for Gumucio's release. On Friday, Gumucio's wife briefly appeared on the roof of a nearby building training binoculars on the residence.

A relaxed-looking Fujimori wearing blue jeans, stopped in the Andean town of Puno to inaugurate public works before flying to Bolivia. His 24-hour visit to the nation with close ethnic and historical ties to Peru came as talks to free the hostages have been shrouded in secrecy.
"We are moving forward in the conversations. I don't have much more than that to tell you," a mediator, Archbishop Juan Luis Cipriani said late on Thursday.
Cipriani and another member of a three-man mediation team, Canadian Ambassador Anthony Vincent, visited the mansion on Thursday for talks with MRTA commander Nestor Cerpa.

Visits by the mediators have become an almost daily occurrence, and lately Cipriani has spoken in a tired, frustrated tone to describe them. There is no date for a resumption of direct talks between the government and the rebels, broken off on March 12.
Canada's Foreign Minister Lloyd Axworthy said on Friday he saw no early solution to the standoff, but underscored his government's willingness to help resolve the crisis.
"I don't see any breakthrough," Lloyd said in Tokyo, where he was completing a 24-hour visit. "There is no magic answer."
Talks reportedly stalled on the issue of MRTA's demand for freedom for some 450 captured comrades in Peruvian jails in exchange for the hostages.

A secret intelligence report obtained by Reuters said new information suggested Congress President Victor Joy Way, two legislators and five mayors -- all harsh critics of the MRTA -- might be targeted for attacks by rebel commandos.
Joy Way was expected to fly to Tokyo this month for hostage crisis talks with Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto.

At noon on Friday, some 50 retired policemen marched past the residence demanding the release of captive comrades. The heads of the police anti-terrotist and intelligence units were among those being held.

The health of a few of the hostages was reported to be deteriorating. All of them were men, mostly in their 40s and 50s, and some suffered from hypertension, diabetes and other chronic diseases, as well as stress-related disorders.
Red Cross officials were seen carrying what looked like an electric cardiogram and boxes of medicines into the residence on Thursday.

The hostages and their families were allowed to exchange mail regularly, though it was read and sometimes censored by the MRTA and government authorities, news reports said. The Red Cross said 8,094 pieces of mail or messages have been carried back and forth since the siege began.
Two dozen of the captives were Japanese, including Tokyo's Ambassador Morihisa Aoki and top Japanese businessmen.

Government officials denied a newspaper report that members of the mediation team had carried a farewell message from Cerpa to his jailed wife, Nancy Gilvonio, who is serving a life term for involvement in MRTA activities, in the assumption that the crisis was headed for a violent ending.
